Abstract
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) en-
hances large language models with external
evidence, but in compliance-oriented QA, se-
mantic relevance alone does not determine
whether evidence should be used for genera-
tion. A retrieved document may be relevant
and factually correct, yet inadmissible because
it is inaccessible to the current user, explic-
itly superseded, or in unresolved conflict with
other active evidence. We formalize three post-
retrieval governance failures in this setting:
unauthorized leakage, stale citation, and un-
supported answers. To address them, we pro-
pose TrustRAG, a RAG framework that incor-
porates a metadata-governed routing layer be-
tween the retriever and the generator. Given
correct and complete governance metadata for
the retrieved candidate set, this layer filters
inadmissible evidence before generation, re-
turns a deterministic refusal when no admis-
sible evidence remains, and preserves unre-
solved conflicts for conflict-reporting genera-
tion. We construct AeroTrustBench, a coun-
terfactual compliance QA benchmark for eval-
uating evidence governance in RAG. Across
Qwen-Max, DeepSeek-V3, and GLM-4-32B-
0414, TrustRAG consistently reduces the three
failures relative to unguided RAG and baselines
based on prompting, filtering, routing, verifica-
tion, and recency. Mechanism-matched and 50-
document comparisons show benefits beyond
filtering under larger candidate pools, while
metadata-noise tests and human audits charac-
terize dependencies on upstream metadata and
evaluator choice.

(RAG) effectively mitigates this issue by incorpo-
rating external documentary evidence (Lewis et al.,
2020). However, compliance-oriented QA requires
RAG to not only consider the semantic relevance
of retrieved evidence but also determine whether
that evidence can be utilized to generate an answer
for the current task. Unlike open-domain RAG, a
document may be semantically relevant and factu-
ally correct, yet remain inadmissible under strict
compliance policies.

Related Work
2.1
Access Control in Compliance-Oriented
QA
Access control is a foundational pillar of security
systems. Resource accessibility depends on at-
tributes like the subject, resource, operation, and
environment, rather than the semantic relevance to
a user’s query (Hu et al., 2014). This distinction
is vital in compliance QA and sensitive domains
with strict confidentiality requirements. Recent
studies have introduced fine-grained access con-
trol into RAG systems, ensuring LLMs generate
answers strictly from documents permitted by the
user’s current privileges (Chen et al., 2025; Gokhan
et al., 2025). For instance, Permission-Aware RAG
handles complex, fine-grained access in enterprise
environments via Identity and Access Management
(IAM) interfaces (Jeong and Lee, 2025), while
Metadata-Aware RAG combines metadata filter-
ing with Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) to
strengthen access enforcement in sensitive data
scenarios (Chen and Taipalus, 2026). These stud-
ies demonstrate the necessity of permission-aware
control boundaries in compliance-oriented RAG.
Building on this, TrustRAG advances post-retrieval
governance by focusing on user permissions, docu-
ment lifecycle states, and conflicting relationships
among legitimate evidence.
2.2
Temporal Freshness and Outdated
Evidence
While RAG effectively mitigates parametric knowl-
edge obsolescence, it does not inherently guarantee
the temporal reliability of retrieved evidence. In
dynamic environments, outdated evidence can mis-
lead generative models and severely degrade per-
formance (Ouyang et al., 2025). For time-sensitive
QA, systems must identify target temporal con-
straints or currently valid facts rather than relying
solely on semantic similarity (Zhang et al., 2025b;
Kasai et al., 2023; Dhingra et al., 2022). Exist-
ing approaches tackle this challenge via two main
mechanisms. One line of research enables mod-
els to adapt to new knowledge through continuous
data updates, search augmentation, or real-time
information acquisition (Liska et al., 2022; Kasai
et al., 2023; Vu et al., 2024). Another focuses on
improving temporal evidence selection via time-
sensitive retrieval, query decomposition, and tem-
poral reranking (Zhang et al., 2025b; Dhingra et al.,
2022). While these methods emphasize acquiring
recent or time-relevant evidence, our work focuses
on strictly governing the validity of retrieved ev-
idence prior to generation by evaluating explicit
document versions and obsolescence states.

3
Methodology
TrustRAG is a metadata-governed RAG frame-
work for compliance-oriented QA, following the
principle of governance before generation. The
framework inserts a metadata-governed routing
layer between the retriever and the language model.
The Governance Router performs metadata nor-
malization, supersession routing, and access filter-
ing before generation, while a conflict-reporting
generation policy instructs the model to report un-
resolved conflicts among retained evidence.
3.1
Task Definition, Response States, and
Failure Taxonomy
Given a user query q, a retrieved candidate doc-
ument set D = {d1, . . . , dn}, and a user per-
mission level r, the system outputs a governed
response y.
Each document is represented as
di = (ci, mi), where ci is the document text
and mi = ⟨idi, li, ti, si⟩is its governance meta-
data. Here, idi is the document identifier, li spec-
ifies the required access level, ti records the doc-
ument timestamp, and si is an explicit superses-
sion pointer. TrustRAG retains ti as metadata, but
does not infer supersession from timestamp order.
If si = idj, then di explicitly supersedes dj; if
si = ⊥, no supersession relation is declared.
For the ordered access levels used in our experi-
ments, the access predicate is defined as:
can_access(di, r) = 1[rank(r) ≥rank(li)] .
where rank(·) maps a user role or document access
level to its position in the access hierarchy.
TrustRAG
defines
three
response
states.
ANSWER indicates that accessible and non-
superseded evidence supports a unique answer.
REFUSAL is used when no accessible and
non-superseded evidence remains after routing.
CONFLICTREPORT indicates that multiple accessi-
ble and non-superseded documents provide incom-
patible facts, and no explicit supersession relation
resolves the conflict. This definition treats refusal
and conflict reporting as valid task outcomes rather
than generation failures.
We focus on post-retrieval evidence-admission
and response-state issues addressed by the
TrustRAG routing layer, and define the following
three governance failures according to whether
a response is supported by admissible evidence.
Unauthorized leakage occurs when the response
contains a factual claim supported only by access-
denied evidence. Stale citation occurs when the
response uses evidence that has been explicitly su-
perseded. Unsupported answer occurs when the
response gives a single factual answer even though
no admissible evidence is available, or when admis-
sible evidence contains an unresolved conflict that
should be reported. Thus, these failures differ from
general answer-quality errors: they are determined
by the relationship between the response and the
evidence allowed under the user role and document
lifecycle metadata.
3.2
TrustRAG Architecture
The TrustRAG architecture decouples retrieval
from generation.
It consists of four functional
modules: Metadata Normalization, Supersession
Routing, Access Filtering, and Conflict-Reporting
Generation. The system operates through two core
paths. The generative path passes filtered admis-
sible evidence to the language model, while the
audit path records the retention or rejection status
of each evidence document, together with its rejec-
tion reasons, to support automatic evaluation and
human inspection. The complete execution flow is
shown in Algorithm 1.

TrustRAG is a metadata-governed RAG frame-

should be reported. Thus, these failures differ from

design holds gold-evidence recall fixed to isolate
evidence governance and final-response genera-
tion under enlarged candidate pools. Appendix
Table A1 summarizes the evaluation sets.
Models and Methods. We evaluate TrustRAG us-
ing three representative general-purpose LLMs as
generators: Qwen-Max, DeepSeek-V3, and GLM-

test instances, candidate documents, and evaluation
criteria, with the sampling temperature set to 0.1.
We compare unguided RAG, prompt-only gover-
nance, metadata filtering, LLM-based routing, post-
hoc verification, recency-based reranking, and the
full TrustRAG framework. We additionally imple-

compare them using the same candidate evidence,
generator models, and evaluation protocol. De-
tailed method definitions are provided in Appendix
Table A2, while complete prompt templates, input
and output specifications, and post-processing rules
are provided in Appendix A.2.

failure taxonomy, we report three binary failure-
rate metrics: Leakage Rate, Stale Citation Rate,
and Unsupported Answer Rate. We also report
utility-oriented diagnostics, including answerabil-
ity on admissible cases and over-refusal rate.
We use a governance-aware LLM judge based on
DeepSeek-V3 (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3) for
binary evaluation. Using human annotations from
a 200-response audit as reference labels, we further
evaluate the same responses with Qwen-Max and
GLM-4-32B-0414 as alternative judges, using the
same inputs, judge prompt, sampling temperature,
and post-processing. Agreement is reported sepa-
rately by failure type and judge. We report failure
rates with 95% confidence intervals using 10,000
bootstrap resamples, and use paired McNemar tests
for key comparisons. For API-served models, we
record model identifiers, evaluation dates, prompts,
code, and raw outputs to support auditing and re-
runs.
